idiom_name: hand-written mapper inside an RAII transaction scope
implementation_notes: C++ ships no standard ORM, so the composite is a class that owns its dependent objects and the mapping code is hand-written against a database API. Express the unit of work with an RAII/SBRM guard - the constructor opens the transaction, the destructor rolls back unless commit() was called - which keeps exceptions and early returns from leaving a partial cluster, and let the database's ON DELETE CASCADE handle dependent removal.
pitfalls: A destructor that swallows or throws on rollback failure breaks the guard contract; keep cleanup noexcept and report the original exception.
Dependents must be owned by value or unique_ptr inside the root; a raw pointer graph lets two loaded clusters alias one child and the save writes it twice.
Copying the composite copies the entire cluster and its identity; make roots move-only or give transfer objects an explicit clone.

variants.name: ODB object-relational mapping over the composite class graph
variants.implementation_notes: ODB generates the schema and the persistence code from declarative class headers: annotate the root and its dependents with #pragma db object, model the cluster as a container of dependent objects, and let the generated database API persist, update and load the graph inside one odb::transaction. Choose ODB when a generated, statically typed mapping justifies adding its compiler to the build; a hand-written mapper stays preferable for small clusters or toolchains that cannot adopt code generation.
pitfalls: ODB is a build-time code generator: the compiler step must run in every configuration and in the IDE, and the generated code is a second artifact to keep in sync.
Container relationships are loaded whole unless declared lazy, so loading a root can pull an entire cluster into memory.
